implementation_notes: Swift's actor type is the language-level monitor: an actor is a reference type whose isolated state may only be touched on self, and cross-actor calls become asynchronous messages placed in the actor's mailbox and executed one at a time on its serial executor, so two methods never run concurrently on the same instance. There are no condition variables: a method that must wait for a state change suspends with await - on another actor, a Task, a continuation or an AsyncStream - instead of blocking a thread, and actor reentrancy means the state must be re-validated after every suspension point. This is the default realisation on modern toolchains; before Swift 5.5 the same guarantee was assembled from Foundation locks and dispatch queues.
pitfalls: Actors are reentrant: state read before an await may change across it, so every await is a re-validation point and two-step invariants must be re-checked, not assumed.
Isolation is enforced only for code the compiler can see: @unchecked Sendable types and captured non-Sendable references reopen the data races the actor was meant to remove.

A long synchronous computation inside an actor blocks its executor for every caller; heavy work must be moved out (nonisolated functions, detached tasks) or the object behaves like a single-threaded bottleneck.

variants.name: NSCondition / NSLock with dispatch queues (pre-actor)
variants.implementation_notes: The classic monitor is available through Foundation: NSCondition bundles a mutex with a condition variable (lock/unlock, wait, wait(until:), signal, broadcast), NSLock and NSRecursiveLock are the bare monitor lock, and DispatchQueue.sync or a serial/barrier queue serialises accesses. Use it for synchronous APIs, for code that must build with toolchains older than Swift 5.5, and where the object is called from synchronous code that cannot await; the structure is otherwise the same monitor as in other languages, with the same predicate loop and the same nested-lockout hazard.
pitfalls: NSLock is not recursive and must be unlocked by the same thread that locked it; NSCondition.wait must be called with the lock held and the predicate re-checked after every wakeup.
Blocking a dispatch queue while holding a lock that another queue waits on is a classic deadlock, and DispatchQueue.sync from the queue's own thread traps at runtime.
NSLock reports misuse only by logging, and under Swift 6 strict concurrency a lock-protected class is non-Sendable unless marked @unchecked Sendable deliberately.
